claims.text: Controlled atomic-level disorder promotes nanoscale chemical inhomogeneity in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
Nanoscale chemical inhomogeneity creates local regions of enhanced magnetoelastic coupling.
Enhanced magnetoelastic coupling enables a reversible magnetostructural transition.
The reversible magnetostructural transition produces a strong magnetocaloric response at applied fields below 2 T.
The proposed transition reduces hysteresis while preserving rapid heat exchange and mechanical stability.
Tailored heat treatments or minor alloying additions can induce controlled nanoscale heterogeneity in the atomic distribution.
The induced nanoscale regions have modified magnetic exchange and elastic properties.
The nanoscale chemical inhomogeneities produce localized differences in magnetic exchange interactions and elastic moduli.
The nanoscale regions trigger a concurrent magnetostructural transformation through locally enhanced magnetoelastic coupling.
The concurrent magnetostructural transformation amplifies the low-field magnetocaloric effect and produces a large entropy change.
The modified alloy will have a greater magnetocaloric temperature change per unit field than the homogeneous baseline.
The modified alloy will have lower hysteresis losses than the homogeneous baseline.
The modified alloy will maintain or improve mechanical stability relative to the homogeneous baseline.
The modified alloy will have unchanged or improved thermal conductivity relative to the homogeneous baseline.
Unchanged or improved thermal conductivity will support rapid heat exchange.
The hypothesis should apply within similar compositional families and phase-stability ranges that support magnetostructural transitions.
The hypothesis may not apply when crystalline ordering limits dislocation and nanodomain formation.
The proposed effect is not expected far from the phase-transition temperature region.
